paraphrase: Does the Lord produce the effect all at once or in sequence, depending on karma or not? As he wishes. paraphrase: The 'wretch' of the sūtra is a living man, not a dead one: unwashed, smeared with dirt, with beard, nails and hair grown, without grooming, so that the marks of caste and āśrama are cut off. paraphrase: For each stage the text gives a residence, livelihood, strength, action, purification and gain: first, in the temple, living on alms, with eightfold celibacy as strength, bathing and laughter etc. as action, removal of impurity as purification, and knowledge as gain; second, among people, living on discarded food, closing the doors of the senses and acting like a madman, destruction of sin, the whole of dharma as gain; third, in an empty house or cave, on alms, enduring like cows and deer, study and meditation, the gain of constant union with the god and conquest of the senses; fourth, in the cremation ground, on what comes, remembrance as action, removal of forgetfulness, union with Rudra as gain; fifth, the vigilance, grace, removal of suffering and attainment of the qualities. Verses list five gains (knowledge, austerity, constant union with the god, yoga, arising of the qualities), five impurities (ignorance, demerit, habituation to objects, non-attainment of steadiness, lack of lordship), five means (residence, meditation, restraint of all organs, remembrance, grace) and five places (the dwelling, the world, the empty house, the cremation ground, Rudra).

paraphrase: The first stage is 'manifest' because the Pāśupata sign is made manifest by ash-bathing, lying in ash and the rest; the second 'unmanifest' because birth and the rest are not shown - the sign is hidden and knowledge concealed (the states of feigned madness and folly belong here); the third is 'conquest', aiming at conquest of the senses; the fourth ends in 'cutting'; the fifth, 'completion', is the total cessation of all the practitioner's activity. paraphrase: 'Residence' names the disciple's faculties of grasping, retaining, inferring, rejecting, understanding, speaking, service and application. Observance (caryā) - from ash-bathing to feigned folly - has three limbs: gift (self-offering to the Lord with prostrations while repeating the five mantras), worship (doing the prescribed acts as the Lord's command) and austerity (bearing the three sufferings without remedy); it is twofold, vows and 'doors'. Daily, at the three junctures, he bathes in consecrated ash while muttering, enters the temple, sits south of the image, mutters, laughs loudly again and again, sings and dances, makes the huḍukkāra, prostrates and mutters; muttering and prostration are mental, dance bodily, laughter, song and huḍukkāra vocal. He then reports the offering, circumambulates, takes the closing bath and salutes the tīrthakaras from Lakulīśa to Rāśīkara.

The power of seeing is fivefold (seeing, hearing, thinking, knowing all treatises, omniscience); the power of acting threefold (swiftness of mind, taking forms at will, acting without organs).

paraphrase: The dependent effect is threefold: vidyā (a quality of the paśu, cognitive or not), kalā (insentient, dependent on the sentient: ten 'effects' - five elements and five qualities - and thirteen 'instruments' - ten senses and the inner organs buddhi, ahaṃkāra and manas), and paśu (with or without body and organs). Yoga is the link of self and Lord through the mind, either as action (muttering, meditation) or as cessation of action. The rule is primary (the observance: vows - ash-bathing, lying in ash, offering, muttering, circumambulation - and the six 'doors': krāthana, spandana, mandana, śṛṅgāraṇa, avitatkaraṇa, avitadbhāṣaṇa) or secondary (re-bathing etc.).

paraphrase: Objection: if the Lord were an independent cause, karma would be fruitless and all effects would arise at once. Reply: karma favoured by the Lord's will bears fruit, and without it may be fruitless, as with Yayāti's; beings act because they depend on his will; he, whose desires are fulfilled, needs nothing that karma produces; and effects do not arise all at once, because his unimpeded power of action follows his will. As the knowers of the tradition say: 'Since he acts by his own will, independent of karma and the rest, he is called in scripture the cause of all causes.'

paraphrase: The Naiyāyikas, also called Yaugas, carry staffs, wear a loincloth and blanket, have matted hair, smear ash, wear the sacred thread and carry water-pots, live mostly in forests on roots and fruits, some with wives and some without (the latter being best), and the most advanced go naked; they greet with 'oṃ namaḥ śivāya'. Their god Īśvara, omniscient maker and destroyer, has eighteen avatāras worshipped as tīrtheśas: Nakulīśa, Kauśika, Gārgya, Maitrya, Kauruṣa, Īśāna, Pāragārgya, Kapilāṇḍa, Manuṣyaka, Kuśika, Atri, Piṅgala, Puṣpaka, Bṛhadārya, Agasti, Santāna, Rāśīkara and Vidyāguru. They say: 'Whoever serves the Śaiva initiation for twelve years and then leaves it - even a slave woman or slave - attains nirvāṇa.'

paraphrase: These ascetics are of four kinds by their conduct - Śaivas, Pāśupatas, Mahāvratadharas and, fourth, Kālamukhas - with subgroups such as bharaṭas, bhaktas, laiṅgikas and tāpasas; for bharaṭas and the like there is no rule of varṇa in taking the vow - whoever has devotion to Śiva may take it. In the treatises the Naiyāyikas are called Śaivas and the Vaiśeṣikas Pāśupatas.

paraphrase: The Śaiva (Yauga) ascetics' god Śaṅkara has eighteen avatāras whom they worship at every step as tīrtheśas - from Nakulīśa, Kauśika, Gārgya, Maitrya and Kauruṣa to Rāśīkara (seventeenth) and Vidyāguru; Akṣapāda is their guru; bharaṭas of any varṇa who have devotion to Śiva take the vow and serve as priests in all their tīrthas.
